title: A Policy Discussion: Complex Relative Clause Structures

dialogue.speaker: Moderator
dialogue.text: We're here to discuss the new curriculum framework. Let me start with the most debated question: which subjects should be compulsory at university level?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I'd argue for English — and specifically, for a model of English instruction that goes beyond grammar drills. The skills that employers consistently value are communication and critical thinking. Any curriculum that doesn't include these isn't preparing students for the world they're entering.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: I agree. But I'd add physical education, which is consistently undervalued in post-secondary systems. The research on physical activity and cognitive performance, which has been accumulating for decades, makes a compelling case.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: Both of those are important. I'd also argue for a civic education component — the kind of course in which students learn about their legal rights, the institutions through which policy is made, and the obligations that citizenship involves.

dialogue.speaker: Moderator
dialogue.text: Amir, what does "communication" mean in the context you're describing?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: It means the ability to explain complex ideas in clear language — to audiences who don't share your technical background. The engineer who can only talk to other engineers is at a disadvantage in a world where collaboration across disciplines is essential.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: Which is exactly why interdisciplinary courses are valuable. A module in which a biologist works alongside a lawyer and an economist to solve a shared problem is the kind of learning environment that develops these skills.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: And civic education, in the form I'm proposing, isn't about political parties — it's about the structures through which society organises itself. That's knowledge that every citizen needs, regardless of the field they enter.

dialogue.speaker: Moderator
dialogue.text: Are there subjects that you think universities have traditionally valued too highly?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Memorisation of content that can be looked up. The student who has memorised 500 facts but who can't explain how those facts connect is less equipped than the student who has memorised fewer facts but who can reason clearly about what they know.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: The skill that universities should be producing — the ability to evaluate evidence critically — is one that cuts across all disciplines. That's what the curriculum should be built around.

questions.text: "Any curriculum that doesn't include these isn't preparing students." — type:
questions.hint: "That" + no commas = defining clause. "Any curriculum THAT..." = tells us which curriculum (the kind that doesn't include them). ✅

questions.text: "Physical education, which is consistently undervalued, has compelling research." — type:
opts: Non-defining — physical education already identified; commas + which
questions.correct: Non-defining — physical education already identified; commas + which
questions.hint: Commas + "which" = non-defining. "Physical education" already identified; the clause adds extra info. ✅

questions.text: "A module in which a biologist works alongside a lawyer." — "in which" is:
questions.hint: "in which" = formal structure. "A module IN WHICH X happens." = "a module where X happens" (informal). ✅

questions.text: "The student ___ can't explain how facts connect is less equipped." (relative pronoun)
questions.hint: People → WHO. "The student WHO can't explain how facts connect." ✅
